title: CDS — English | Tenses
description: Subject-wise test on Tenses (English) for CDS. 40Q.
subject: cds-english

questions.question: My brother has gone to Mumbai yesterday. Identify the error.

options.explanation: Not an error
Should be 'went'
Not an error
There is an error

questions.explanation: The adverb 'yesterday' specifies a definite time in the past, which requires the simple past tense. Therefore, 'has gone' should be replaced with 'went'.
questions.subject: cds-english

questions.question: She is studying for her exams since morning. Improve the sentence.

options.explanation: Correct form
Incorrect tense
Incorrect tense
Incorrect tense

questions.explanation: The phrase 'since morning' indicates an action that started in the past and is continuing up to the present. This requires the present perfect continuous tense ('has been studying').
questions.subject: cds-english

questions.question: If I was a bird, I would fly across the sky. Identify the error.

options.explanation: Should be 'were'
Not an error
Not an error
There is an error

questions.explanation: In hypothetical conditional sentences (Type 2) expressing an unreal or imaginary situation in the present, 'were' is used for all subjects, including 'I', 'he', 'she', 'it'. Thus, 'was' should be 'were'.
questions.subject: cds-english

questions.question: The patient died before the doctor arrived. Improve the sentence.

options.explanation: Correct form
Incorrect tense
Incorrect tense
Incorrect tense

questions.explanation: When two actions happened in the past, the action that occurred earlier is expressed in the past perfect tense, and the later action is in the simple past tense. Here, the patient's death occurred before the doctor's arrival.
questions.subject: cds-english

questions.question: He is owning a large estate in the countryside. Identify the error.

options.explanation: Should be 'owns'
Not an error
Not an error
There is an error

questions.explanation: 'Own' is a stative verb (a verb that describes a state rather than an action) and is generally not used in continuous tenses. The correct form is the simple present tense, 'He owns'.
questions.subject: cds-english

questions.question: Scarcely had I reached the station than the train departed. Identify the error.

options.explanation: Not an error
Should be 'when'
Not an error
There is an error

questions.explanation: The correlative conjunction pair for 'Scarcely' is 'when' or 'before', not 'than'. The correct phrase should be 'Scarcely had I reached the station when the train departed.'
questions.subject: cds-english

questions.question: By the time he finishes his speech, the audience will leave. Improve the sentence.

options.explanation: Correct form
Incorrect tense
Incorrect tense
Incorrect tense

questions.explanation: This sentence describes an action that will be completed before a specific point in the future ('by the time he finishes his speech'). This requires the future perfect tense ('will have left').
questions.subject: cds-english

questions.question: I am living in this city for five years. Identify the error.

options.explanation: Should be 'have been living'
Not an error
Not an error
There is an error

questions.explanation: The phrase 'for five years' indicates a duration, implying an action that started in the past and continues up to the present. This requires the present perfect continuous tense ('I have been living').
questions.subject: cds-english

questions.question: If you had informed me earlier, I will have attended the meeting. Improve the sentence.

options.explanation: Correct form
Incorrect tense
Incorrect tense
Incorrect tense

questions.explanation: This is a Type 3 conditional sentence, which describes an unreal past condition and its probable past result. The structure is: If + Past Perfect, Subject + would have + Past Participle. Therefore, 'will have attended' should be 'would have attended'.
questions.subject: cds-english

questions.question: The teacher asked the students if they have understood the lesson. Identify the error.

options.explanation: Not an error
Should be 'had understood'
Not an error
There is an error

questions.explanation: This sentence demonstrates the sequence of tenses in reported speech. Since the reporting verb 'asked' is in the simple past tense, the tense in the reported clause must be shifted back accordingly. 'Have understood' (present perfect) should change to 'had understood' (past perfect).
questions.subject: cds-english

questions.question: She is studying for her exams since morning.

options.explanation: The present continuous tense is incorrect here.
This part of the sentence is grammatically correct.
The use of 'since morning' requires the present perfect continuous tense.
There is an error in the sentence.

questions.explanation: The phrase 'since morning' indicates an action that started in the past and is continuing up to the present. For such actions, the present perfect continuous tense ('has been studying') is required, not the present continuous tense ('is studying').
questions.subject: cds-english

questions.question: I didn't see him since he left for Delhi last month.

options.explanation: The present perfect tense is correct here.
The past perfect tense is not required in this context.
The past continuous tense is not relevant here.
The sentence can be improved.

questions.explanation: The word 'since' connects a past point in time ('he left for Delhi last month') to the present. When an action began in the past and continues or has relevance up to the present, the present perfect tense ('haven't seen') is used.
questions.subject: cds-english

questions.question: By the time we reached the theatre, the movie already began.

options.explanation: This part of the sentence is grammatically correct.
This part of the sentence is grammatically correct.
The past perfect tense ('had already begun') is required here.
There is an error in the sentence.

questions.explanation: When two actions occurred in the past, and one happened before the other, the earlier action is expressed in the past perfect tense, and the later action in the simple past.
questions.subject: cds-english

questions.question: If it will rain tomorrow, the match will be cancelled.

options.explanation: The simple present tense is correct in the 'if' clause.
The conditional tense is not required in the 'if' clause.
The past perfect tense is not relevant in this context.
The sentence can be improved.

questions.explanation: This is a Type 1 conditional sentence, which deals with a possible condition and its probable result. In such sentences, the 'if' clause (conditional clause) uses the simple present tense, while the main clause uses the simple future tense.
questions.subject: cds-english

questions.question: The captain announced that the team is practicing hard for the upcoming tournament.

options.explanation: This part of the sentence is grammatically correct.
The verb 'is practicing' should be in the past tense ('was practicing').
This part of the sentence is grammatically correct.
There is an error in the sentence.

questions.explanation: This sentence demonstrates the rule of sequence of tenses in reported speech. The main verb 'announced' is in the simple past. Therefore, the verb in the subordinate clause ('is practicing') must also be in a corresponding past tense.
questions.subject: cds-english

questions.question: She is teaching English in this school for the past five years.

options.explanation: The present perfect continuous tense is correct here.
The past perfect continuous tense is not relevant in this context.
The past continuous tense is not relevant in this context.
The sentence can be improved.

questions.explanation: The phrase 'for the past five years' indicates an action that started five years ago and is still continuing in the present. This requires the present perfect continuous tense ('has been teaching'), not the present continuous tense ('is teaching').

questions.question: I am knowing him for five years, but I still don't understand his motives. Identify the correct sentence.

Incorrect verb form
Incorrect verb form

questions.explanation: The verb 'know' is a stative verb and is generally not used in continuous tenses. When referring to a duration up to the present, the present perfect tense is appropriate.

questions.question: The concert has started an hour ago. Which part of the sentence contains the error?

options.explanation: The subject of the sentence is 'The concert', which is correct.
The verb 'has started' is in the present perfect tense, which is incorrect in this context.
The phrase 'an hour ago' is correct, as it indicates a specific point in the past.
There is an error in the sentence, which is the use of the present perfect tense 'has started'.

questions.explanation: The phrase 'an hour ago' indicates a specific point in the past, requiring the simple past tense. 'Has started' is present perfect. The correct form should be 'started'.

questions.question: If I was a bird, I would fly. Which of the following is the correct sentence?

options.text: If I am a bird, I would fly.
options.explanation: The sentence 'If I am a bird' is in the present tense, which is not suitable for a hypothetical situation.

options.text: If I were a bird, I would fly.
options.explanation: The sentence 'If I were a bird' uses the subjunctive mood 'were', which is correct for a hypothetical situation.

options.text: If I had been a bird, I would fly.
options.explanation: The sentence 'If I had been a bird' is in the past perfect tense, which is not suitable for a hypothetical situation in the present or future.

options.text: If I will be a bird, I would fly.
options.explanation: The sentence 'If I will be a bird' is in the future tense, which is not suitable for a hypothetical situation.

questions.explanation: This is a hypothetical conditional sentence (Type 2) where the subjunctive mood 'were' is used for unreal or improbable situations in the present or future, regardless of the subject's number.
questions.subject: cds-english

questions.question: She usually go to bed at 10 PM. Which part of the sentence contains the error?

options.explanation: The subject of the sentence is 'She', which is correct.
The verb 'go' does not agree in number with the subject 'She', which is a third-person singular.
The phrase 'to bed' is correct, as it indicates the action of going to bed.
The phrase 'at 10 PM' is correct, as it indicates the time of the action.

questions.explanation: For a habitual action in the simple present tense with a third-person singular subject ('She'), the verb must agree in number. 'Go' should be 'goes'.
questions.subject: cds-english

questions.question: By the time we reached the station, the train already left. Which of the following is the correct sentence?

options.explanation: The sentence 'the train already leaves' is in the present tense, which is not suitable for a past action.
The sentence 'the train already has left' is in the present perfect tense, which is not suitable for a past action that occurred before another past action.
The sentence 'the train had already left' uses the past perfect tense, which is correct for an action that occurred before another past action.
The sentence 'the train already leaving' is in the present participle form, which is not suitable for a past action.

questions.explanation: When two actions happened in the past, the action that occurred first is expressed in the past perfect tense, and the later action in the simple past. The train leaving happened before we reached the station.
questions.subject: cds-english

questions.question: I have been living in this city since five years. Which part of the sentence contains the error?

options.explanation: The phrase 'I have been living' is correct, as it indicates the action of living in the city.
The phrase 'in this city' is correct, as it indicates the location of the action.
The phrase 'since five years' is incorrect, as 'since' should be used with a point in time, not a period of time.
There is an error in the sentence, which is the use of 'since' with a period of time.

questions.explanation: 'Since' is used with a point in time (e.g., since 2018, since Monday). 'For' is used with a period of time (e.g., for five years, for two months). Therefore, 'since five years' should be 'for five years'.
questions.subject: cds-english

questions.question: The principal announced that the exams will be postponed. Which part of the sentence contains the error?

options.explanation: The phrase 'The principal announced' is correct, as it indicates the action of announcing.
The phrase 'that the exams' is correct, as it indicates the subject of the reported clause.
The verb 'will be postponed' is in the future tense, which is not suitable for a reported speech sentence with a past tense reporting verb.
There is an error in the sentence, which is the use of the future tense 'will be postponed' in a reported speech sentence with a past tense reporting verb.

questions.explanation: This is a reported speech sentence. When the reporting verb ('announced') is in the past tense, the verb in the reported clause typically shifts to a corresponding past tense. 'Will be' should change to 'would be'.
questions.subject: cds-english

questions.question: Hardly had I stepped out of my house than I saw a strange incident. Which of the following is the correct sentence?

options.text: Hardly had I stepped out of my house when I saw a strange incident.
options.explanation: The sentence 'Hardly had I stepped out of my house when I saw a strange incident' uses the correct correlative conjunction 'hardly...when'.

options.text: Hardly I had stepped out of my house when I saw a strange incident.
options.explanation: The sentence 'Hardly I had stepped out of my house' is incorrect, as it does not use the correct correlative conjunction.

options.text: I had hardly stepped out of my house than I saw a strange incident.
options.explanation: The sentence 'I had hardly stepped out of my house' is incorrect, as it does not use the correct correlative conjunction.

options.text: Hardly had I stepped out of my house then I saw a strange incident.
options.explanation: The sentence 'Hardly had I stepped out of my house then' is incorrect, as it uses the incorrect word 'then' instead of 'when'.

questions.explanation: The correlative conjunction 'hardly...when' (or 'scarcely...when') is used to express that one event immediately followed another. 'Than' is incorrect in this context; it is used with 'no sooner...than'.
questions.subject: cds-english

questions.question: If he would have studied harder, he would have passed the exam easily. Which part of the sentence contains the error?

options.explanation: The phrase 'If he would have studied' is incorrect, as it uses the incorrect 'would have' + past participle instead of the past perfect tense.
The word 'harder' is correct, as it indicates the degree of studying.
The phrase 'he would have passed' is correct, as it indicates the hypothetical result of the action.
The phrase 'the exam easily' is correct, as it indicates the object and manner of the action.

questions.explanation: This is a Type 3 conditional sentence (unreal past). The 'if' clause should use the past perfect tense, not 'would have' + past participle. It should be 'If he had studied harder'.
questions.subject: cds-english

questions.question: They are building a new bridge for the last three years, but it is still not finished. Which of the following is the correct sentence?

options.text: They have built a new bridge for the last three years
options.explanation: The sentence 'They have built a new bridge' is in the present perfect tense, which indicates a completed action, but the phrase 'for the last three years' indicates an ongoing action.

options.text: They have been building a new bridge for the last three years
options.explanation: The sentence 'They have been building a new bridge' uses the present perfect continuous tense, which is correct for an action that started in the past and is still continuing.

options.text: They build a new bridge for the last three years
options.explanation: The sentence 'They build a new bridge' is in the simple present tense, which is not suitable for an action that started in the past and is still continuing.

options.text: They had built a new bridge for the last three years
options.explanation: The sentence 'They had built a new bridge' is in the past perfect tense, which indicates a completed action in the past, but the phrase 'for the last three years' indicates an ongoing action.

questions.explanation: The phrase 'for the last three years' indicates an action that started in the past and is still continuing in the present. This requires the present perfect continuous tense ('have been building').
questions.subject: cds-english

questions.question: It is high time you start taking your studies seriously. Which part of the sentence contains the error?

options.explanation: The phrase 'It is high time' is correct, as it indicates the necessity of the action.
The verb 'you start' is in the present tense, which is not suitable for the expression 'It is high time'.
The phrase 'taking your studies' is correct, as it indicates the object of the action.
The word 'seriously' is correct, as it indicates the manner of the action.

questions.explanation: The expression 'It is high time' or 'It is time' is followed by the simple past tense, even though it refers to a present or future action, to indicate that an action should have already started or should start immediately. So, 'you start' should be 'you started'.

questions.question: By the time the rescue team arrived, the injured climber was freezing for several hours. Choose the best option to replace the underlined part of the sentence.

options.explanation: The past continuous tense does not convey the duration leading up to the arrival.
The past perfect continuous tense correctly conveys the duration leading up to the arrival.
The simple past tense implies a completed action without duration.
The past perfect tense indicates a completed action before another past action, but does not convey the ongoing nature leading up to the arrival.

questions.explanation: The sentence describes an action (freezing) that started in the past and continued for a duration ('for several hours') up to another point in the past ('By the time the rescue team arrived'). This requires the past perfect continuous tense.
